cur:catacombs-cyriaca-christ-saints.summary: Wilpert's plate shows a painted arcosolium: in the lunette Christ sits among saints, while scenes of Moses and Jonah appear on the surrounding wall and arch. The tomb places its occupant under the protection of Christ enthroned in the company of the saints.
facts: Wilpert's caption reads 'Moses, Jonah, Christ with saints'.
The catacomb of Cyriaca lies beneath San Lorenzo fuori le mura; Italian Wikipedia notes that wartime bombing and the Verano cemetery have left it in poor condition.
Painting reproduced from Joseph Wilpert, Die Malereien der Katakomben Roms (Freiburg, 1903), whose plates were photographed in the catacombs and hand-coloured in front of the originals.
cur:catacombs-cyriaca-christ-saints.notes: The plate is small and the central figures are hard to read; date approximate.

walters:54.59.summary: Christ stands on this bronze pectoral cross in a long sleeveless tunic, his arms spread along the cross-arms and his head framed by a cross-nimbus, while small figures of the Virgin and St John appear at the ends of the arms. Greek inscriptions on the arms give his words from the cross, 'Behold your son' and 'Behold your mother'. Such crosses were worn on the breast and held a relic within.
facts: The Walters records the inscription on the horizontal arms as 'Behold your mother, Behold your son'.
Henry Walters bought the cross from the dealer Joseph Brummer in 1925; the museum dates it to the 10th–11th century.
walters:54.59.notes: Image viewed on the Walters image server. The identity of the small figures on the arms follows the inscription.

wga:zearly/1/4mosaics/1rome/4cosma/cosma.summary: Against a deep blue sky streaked with fiery sunset clouds, a majestic, bearded Christ in golden robes descends as if walking down a staircase of cloud, his right hand raised, while Saints Peter and Paul present the physician-martyrs Cosmas and Damian to him, joined by Saint Theodore and Pope Felix IV. It is one of the most dramatic apse mosaics of Rome, an image of the Lord's return in glory set above the old Roman Forum. Its monumental, almost tangible Christ became a model for Roman apses for centuries.
facts: Pope Felix IV (526–530) created the basilica in 527 from buildings of the ancient Forum of Peace given by the Ostrogothic rulers Theodoric and Amalasuntha; it is often called the first church in the Roman Forum.
Below the main scene, twelve lambs approach the Lamb of God on a hill from which the four rivers of Paradise flow, symbolising the apostles and the faithful.
The phoenix perched on the palm tree at the left is an ancient emblem of resurrection.

The figure of Pope Felix holding a model of the church is largely the work of later restorers, and the arch was cut down in the 17th-century rebuilding, but the central composition is essentially sixth-century work.
wga:zearly/1/4mosaics/1rome/4cosma/cosma.notes: Dated 526–530 (pontificate of Felix IV). Wikipedia calls the church's mosaics 'much restored'; the precise extent of later restoration (e.g. of the Felix IV figure) was not verified here. WGA's statement that Christ wears a crown is not borne out by the image and was not repeated.
